character_facts: The masked master is female, since the attendant addresses her as 'milady'.
The bio-mother is physically failing and appears dependent on tubes and a respirator-like mask.
The bio-mother expects to die during the delivery.
The bio-mother loved a man described as a poet.
The master is connected to the Castaka bloodline or clan through the unborn boy.
continuity_links: The page centers on succession and bloodline questions within the Castaka/Metabaron lineage.
The mention of Krleza and the poet-lover points to an earlier relationship affecting the twins' parentage.
dialogue_meaning: The scene is a forced choice between the survival of one twin or the other.
The mother believes lineage and clan duty should make the master's decision favor the boy.
The boy is framed as belonging to the master's hereditary line.
The girl is emotionally associated with the mother's lover and an alternative future.
The master tests whether the mother would reject clan expectations if the girl were chosen.
locations: a medical or birthing chamber filled with machinery and life-support equipment
lore_facts: Castaka can sire only male children, according to the mother's statement.
Krleza is identified as the origin or affiliation connected to the girl and the man the mother loves.
The title or role 'Metabaron' is associated with raising boys as pitiless warriors, according to the mother's description.
The setting includes advanced reproductive or surgical technology capable of monitoring and attempting a selective delivery.
plot_events: A medical attendant announces that the pregnant woman carries twins, one girl and one boy.
The attendant states the mother's condition is too weak to deliver both children and only one infant can be saved.
The mother insists the master will choose to save the boy.
She explains the boy is the master's because Castaka can sire only male children.
She says the girl is linked to Krleza and to the man she loves.
The mother argues that if the boy lives he will be raised as a pitiless warrior, while she herself expects to die in childbirth.
The master asks what would happen if the girl were saved instead.
The mother replies that the daughter of her poet-lover would give her strength to live and raise her.
uncertainties: The exact identities and names of the masked master, the bio-mother, and the medical attendant are not given on this page.
The mother's line about the girl being 'from Krleza' is legible in meaning but may contain nuance about parentage or origin that is not fully clear from the page alone.
It is not fully explicit whether 'the man I love' is the girl's biological father, though the dialogue strongly links him to her.
visual_summary: In a dark, mechanical birthing chamber, an armored medical attendant projects an image of twins in the womb while reporting to a masked master. The mother, encased in life-support machinery, is too weak to deliver both infants, so one must be sacrificed. She argues over which child should live: the boy belongs to the master's Castaka line, while the girl is tied to the man she loves. The master questions her about saving the girl, ending on a close-up of the mother answering desperately through her mask.
